note: Starword answers: five letters, each with what you learn when you finish. Guesses can be any common English word (data/words5.txt, from SCOWL). The order is shuffled once with a fixed seed, so a day's word is the same for everyone.
words: The path one body follows around another under gravity. The Moon takes 27.3 days to go once around Earth against the stars.
A lump of ice and dust from the outer Solar System. Near the Sun it grows a coma and tails that can stretch for millions of kilometres.
Of the Moon. From one sunrise to the next, a lunar day lasts about 29.5 Earth days.
Of the Sun. The solar wind streams away from it at roughly 300 to 800 kilometres a second.
The hottest planet: its thick carbon dioxide air holds the surface near 465 °C, hotter than Mercury.
The only world yet known to have life. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach it.
A dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt. New Horizons flew past it on 14 July 2015 and found a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice.
Saturn's largest moon, with air thicker than Earth's and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.
The largest body in the asteroid belt, a dwarf planet that the Dawn spacecraft orbited from 2015 to 2018.
One of the largest asteroids. Dawn orbited it in 2011 and 2012 before moving on to Ceres.
The tail of Cygnus, a white supergiant so luminous it is among the brightest stars in our sky despite lying well over a thousand light-years away.
The blue supergiant at Orion's foot, about 860 light-years away.
The brightest star in Virgo: two hot stars so close they orbit each other every four days.
The star at the bend of the Big Dipper's handle. With faint Alcor beside it, it was an old test of eyesight.
Mizar's faint companion in the handle of the Big Dipper.
The Demon Star in Perseus, which dims for about ten hours every 2.87 days when a fainter companion passes in front of it.
The brightest star of the Southern Cross.
Beta Centauri, one of the two Pointers that lead the eye to the Southern Cross.
One of the Big Dipper's Pointers: follow it from Merak and you reach Polaris.
The other Pointer of the Big Dipper. A line from Merak through Dubhe leads to the North Star.
The fainter of Orion's two feet, opposite Rigel.
The ram. The 'first point of Aries', where the Sun crosses the celestial equator in March, has drifted into Pisces as Earth's axis wobbles.
The scales: the only constellation of the zodiac that is not a living thing.
The second-largest constellation, and home of the Virgo Cluster of galaxies, about 54 million light-years away.
The dragon that winds around the north celestial pole. Its star Thuban was the pole star when the pyramids were built.
The largest of the 88 constellations: a water snake more than 100 degrees long.
The hunter, home of Betelgeuse, Rigel and the Orion Nebula, a nursery of new stars 1,344 light-years away.
The sea monster, home of Mira, a star that brightens and fades over about eleven months.
The wolf. In 1006 the brightest supernova on record appeared in Lupus.
The table, named for Table Mountain above Cape Town: the faintest constellation, though part of the Large Magellanic Cloud lies in it.
The carpenter's square, a small southern constellation lying across the Milky Way.
The mariner's compass, one of the southern constellations Lacaille added in the 1750s.
A southern constellation added by Dutch navigators in the 1590s.
Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks, held together by gluons.
A particle with whole-number spin, like the photon. The Higgs boson was found at CERN in 2012.
The particle that carries the strong force, binding quarks into protons and neutrons.
Lasers fired at reflectors that Apollo crews left on the Moon measure its distance to within millimetres.
Radar echoes bounced off Venus in the 1960s fixed the length of the astronomical unit, the distance from Earth to the Sun.
An uncrewed spacecraft sent to study another world up close.
A vehicle that drives across another world. Opportunity covered more than 45 kilometres of Mars.
A pass close to a world without stopping. Voyager 2 flew by all four giant planets.
The dark 'seas' of the Moon: plains of old lava, not water. One is a mare.
A huge impact crater. The Moon's South Pole–Aitken basin is about 2,500 kilometres across.
A long, narrow channel on the Moon, often a collapsed lava tube.
All four giant planets have rings; Saturn's are by far the brightest.
Saturn has more known moons than any other planet: over 270.
About 9,000 stars are bright enough to see without a telescope, counting both hemispheres.
A small star, like a red or white dwarf, or a small planet, like Pluto or Ceres.
A star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its old size.
A sudden burst of energy on the Sun, graded A, B, C, M or X by how brightly it shines in X-rays.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been watched since at least the 1830s.
The point directly beneath you, opposite the zenith.
The nearest or farthest point of an orbit. Perihelion and aphelion are the two apsides of an orbit around the Sun.
Where an orbit crosses a reference plane. Eclipses happen only when the Moon is near one of its nodes.
The moment for which star positions or orbital elements are given, such as J2000.0.
The Moon's pull raises the tides, and their drag is slowly lengthening Earth's day.
The Kármán line, 100 kilometres up, is one common definition of where space begins.
Vast regions nearly empty of galaxies, tens to hundreds of millions of light-years across.
The faint spheres of old stars and dark matter that surround galaxies.
The crowded centre of a spiral galaxy. The Milky Way's is stretched into a bar.
A pulsar sends out a pulse with every turn, some of them hundreds of times a second.
How much of the Moon's sunlit half faces Earth. It takes 29.5 days to go through every phase.
It covers about 300,000 kilometres every second. Everything you see, you see as it was when its light set out.
Io's volcanoes erupt some of the hottest lava in the Solar System.
The Oort cloud: a shell of icy bodies that may reach more than a light-year from the Sun.
Earth's axial tilt of about 23.4 degrees is what gives us seasons.
Mars has polar caps of water ice, topped in winter with frozen carbon dioxide.
Neptune has the fastest winds measured on any planet, over 2,000 kilometres an hour.
Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions in the universe, seen across billions of light-years.
The brightest star in a constellation is usually given the Greek letter alpha, as in Alpha Centauri.
Omega Centauri, the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way, holds around ten million stars.
Delta-v is the change in velocity a spacecraft must make to reach its target; budgets of it decide every mission.
The Russian spacecraft that has carried crews since 1967, longer than any other design.
A moon of Uranus, named, like most of its sisters, for a character in Shakespeare.
A moon of Saturn found by the astronomer Giovanni Cassini in 1684.
A small inner moon of Jupiter, found in Voyager 1 pictures in 1979.
Jupiter's innermost moon, which goes around in about seven hours.
The Helix Nebula: the shed outer layers of a dying star, about 650 light-years away.
Short for telescope. Galileo first turned one on the sky in 1609.
A prism spreads light into a spectrum, and a star's spectrum shows what it is made of.
An equatorial mount turns a telescope around an axis parallel to Earth's, so one motion follows the stars.
Webb's near-infrared camera has about 40 million pixels across its ten detectors.
Radio astronomy began when Karl Jansky heard the Milky Way crackling in his receiver in 1932.
Gravitational waves were first detected on 14 September 2015, from two black holes merging.
The Very Large Array in New Mexico: 27 dishes working together as one radio telescope.
A small moon that sweeps the edge of Saturn's A ring, and the name of the rocket that carried John Glenn into orbit.
John Glenn, the first American to orbit Earth, aboard Friendship 7 on 20 February 1962.
Carl Sagan asked for Voyager 1 to turn around and photograph Earth: the Pale Blue Dot, 1990.
Tycho Brahe measured the planets so precisely that Kepler could find their laws. A bright crater on the Moon has his name.
Vera Rubin's measurements of how fast galaxies spin were key evidence for dark matter.
Fred Hoyle, who doubted the theory, gave it its name, 'Big Bang', on BBC radio in 1949.
Titan has fields of dunes made of organic grains, some hundreds of kilometres long.
The darkest part of a shadow. During a total solar eclipse you are standing in the Moon's umbra.
To an astronomer every element heavier than helium is a 'metal'.
Drag from the thin upper atmosphere slowly lowers satellites; the space station needs regular boosts to stay up.
The black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, Sagittarius A*, has about four million times the Sun's mass.
Comet Swift–Tuttle sheds the dust of the Perseid meteors every August.
Plural of nova: a white dwarf that flares when gas taken from a companion star ignites on its surface.
The four inner planets are rocky; the four outer ones are giants of gas and ice.
If space went on forever, unchanged, every line of sight would end on a star and the night would be bright. It is dark because the universe had a beginning.
A section of a rocket that drops away when its fuel is spent. The Saturn V had three.
Apollo 13's landing was called off after an oxygen tank exploded; the crew looped around the Moon and came home safely.
From the ground under you to the edge of the observable universe is about 27 powers of ten.
A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
The Sun's activity rises and falls over a cycle of about eleven years.
Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where magnetic fields hold back the heat rising from below.
Enceladus sprays plumes of water out of cracks near its south pole.
Europa very likely hides a salty ocean under its ice, holding more water than all of Earth’s oceans.
Water ice lies in permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
The Local Group: the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum and dozens of small galaxies.
The hydrogen and helium made in the first minutes after the Big Bang are still most of the atoms in the universe.
Redshift: light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths as the space it crosses expands.
The Hubble Deep Field, 1995, found thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a tennis ball seen from 100 metres.
Rocky planets and moons have solid surfaces; Jupiter and Saturn have none to stand on.
The Moon's far side has a thicker crust than its near side, which is one reason it has so few dark maria.
Mars's carbon dioxide frost turns to gas each spring, and the escaping gas carves spidery channels near its south pole.
Coronagraphs block a star's glare so that faint planets or the Sun's corona beside it can be seen.
A pulsar's beams sweep space like a lighthouse's; we see a pulse each time one crosses Earth.
Precession makes Earth's axis drift in a circle every 26,000 years; in about 12,000 years Vega will be the pole star.
Castor and Pollux, the twins of Gemini; Castor is actually six stars bound together.
The Eagle was Apollo 11’s lunar module, which landed on 20 July 1969; the Eagle Nebula holds the Pillars of Creation.
Planetary nebulae are shells of gas shed by dying stars, lit by the hot core left behind.
In 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the asteroid Dimorphos on purpose and shortened its orbit by 32 minutes.
Jupiter’s dark belts and pale zones are bands of cloud running around the planet, each in its own wind.
The cosmic microwave background is the relic glow of the young universe, cooled now to 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.
Parker Solar Probe is the fastest object people have made, passing the Sun at about 690,000 kilometres an hour.
Webb looks so deep into space that it sees galaxies as they were less than 400 million years after the Big Bang.
